newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SOCCER-ENGLAND OFFICIALS SATISFIED AS UEFA BACKS DOWN.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ENGLAND OFFICIALS SATISFIED AS UEFA BACKS DOWN.

text.p: England, who have not beaten Germany in a competitive soccer match since the 1966 World Cup final, were enjoying a satisfying victory off the field against their old rivals on Thursday.

English officials were delighted after a day of meetings in a Geneva hotel which ended with UEFA, European soccer's governing body, publically admitting that England had every right to bid for the finals -- even though UEFA opened a can of worms three months ago by announcing their unilateral support for Germany.

UEFA President Lennart Johansson, his usual jovial, avuncular manner replaced by barely concealed frustration, said while UEFA had had a "gentleman's agreement with Germany" since 1993 and would not break it, they could not, under the present statutes, prevent England from lobbying for the tournament.
"We would rather this was not the case but it is and we have to live with it," UEFA general secretary Gerhard Aigner added.

Johansson said he was "surprised" the English Football Association (F.A.) did not know of UEFA's support for Germany until this February given that former chairman of the F.A. Sir Bert Millichip was at all the meetings at which the issue was discussed.
This point has been a major bone of contention between England and UEFA, as it was never officially recorded in UEFA committee meeting minutes.

But it was this understanding that formed the basis of the "gentlemen's agreement" between UEFA and Germany and led to Thursday's meetings which UEFA called in an effort to find a way out of the muddle they had themselves created.
And while Johansson admitted openly the "gentlemen's agreement" existed, he also said UEFA could not force the English delegation to withdraw their intention to bid.

The agreement with Germany could yet have major repercussions for the English, depending on whether or not a change in the rules relating to bids is enforced when world soccer's governing body FIFA holds its rule-making congress in Paris next June before the start of the World Cup in France.
UEFA's plan, centered on their Vision policy statement for the future of soccer, would mean each confederation within FIFA would agree to submit just one bid from one member nation.

A vote to accept the Vision document will either be accepted or rejected next June. If it is accepted, UEFA's executive committee will urge their members to vote for Germany. If it is rejected there will be nothing to stop England and Germany continuing with their bids until the final decision on where tournament is staged is taken in the summer of 2000.

The matter is further complicated by the fact Johansson, whose support for Germany was made obvious on Thursday, is expected to become FIFA president when Brazilian Joao Havelange retires next summer.
Despite potential problems further down the road, it was the English who were in expansive mood on Thursday.
"I am delighted with what has happened today," F.A. chief executive Graham Kelly said.

"UEFA have upheld our right to bid for the tournament and in fact they have no obligation to do anything else. Under the current statutes they cannot nominate one candidate. They knew they were wrong to do so and we are very pleased UEFA have recognised our position."
Alec McGivan, the director of England's bid, was equally upbeat.
"We now have the green light to contest this bid in a fair and open way. It only renews our enthusiasm for the task."

David Davies, the English F.A.'s director of communications, added: "It was important that UEFA recognised England's position today and they have done so. It was never UEFA's perogative to nominate a single candidate under the present rules. This is the second biggest sporting event on the planet and deserves more than a quiet agreement in a committee room to see it through."
In contrast, German officials left Geneva disappointed.
President of the German F.A. Egidius Braun said Germany had given their support to England to host last June's European championships and expected England's support for their World Cup bid in return.

"This is not the case," he said, "but as far as I am concerned the status quo has not changed so much. Our gentlemen's agreement with UEFA has not been broken and we still believe we have a very firm bid of our own."
Franz Beckenbauer, who captained West Germany to victory in the 1974 World Cup, coached the country to victory in 1990 and who is spearheading the 2006 bid, was also disappointed.
"I believe that this situation will divide the European bid and if two European countries go for it, it could give an advantage to a third country," he said.
South Africa, Egypt, Morocco, Brazil and Argentina have expressed an early interest in staging the finals.
